articles.title: Tamil Nadu: Former DMK minister Anbil Mahesh appears before CCB in over Rs 100-crore private school approval fraud case
articles.description: Former School Education Minister Anbil Mahesh Poyyamozhi on September 18 appeared before the Chennai Central Crime Branch police for questioning in connection with the private school approval fraud case. The DMK leader, against whom the CCB has registered a Prevention of Corruption Act case, was accompanied by his advocates. The CCB in Chennai issued a summons to him on September 18 following extensive eight-hour searches at premises linked to him in Chennai and Trichy on September 16 in connection with an alleged ₹100-crore fraud involving promises of government approval and recognition for private schools. DMK EX-MINISTER ANBIL MAHESH HAS BEEN SUMMONED TO APPEAR BEFORE THE CCB COPS IN CHENNAI ON SEPTEMBER 18 Former state minister Anbil Mahesh Poyyamozhi has been summoned by the Chennai Central Crime Branch (CCB) police to appear before the investigating officers on September 18... pic.twitter.com/CTSp82yOtO — A Selvaraj (@Crime_Selvaraj) September 16, 2026 As many as 118 items, including property deeds, bank statements, 18 mobile phones, laptops and tablets, were seized during the raid, which was initiated following a complaint by a private school association. The police arrested B T Arasakumar and two others in June. Also Read: Tamil Nadu: Ex DMK Minister Senthil Balaji, brother get anticipatory bail in alleged Rs 35 crore TVK MLA bribery case The case stems from a complaint filed by Elangovan, Secretary of the Federation of Associations of Private Schools in Tamil Nadu, with the Chennai City Police Commissioner. He alleged that a network had collected money from private school managements after promising to secure government approvals, including permanent recognition, upgradation, DTCP clearance and other clearances. BIG BREAKING: A case has been registered against former School Education Minister Anbil Mahesh Poyyamozhi under provisions of the Prevention of Corruption Act over alleged corruption and breach of trust. Simultaneous searches are underway at 4 locations linked to him in... pic.twitter.com/ZT3Uz4C07b — Actor Vijay Team (@ActorVijayTeam) September 16, 2026 Central Crime Branch police registered a complaint and arrested the prime accused, BT Arasakumar (59) of Saligramam, Chennai, on June 27. He was later remanded in judicial custody and detained under the Goondas Act. Two other accused have also been arrested in the case. It is learnt that the police have examined over 250 people across Tamil Nadu, including several government officials from the School Education Department, and relevant government documents have been seized. Initial inquiry has revealed that several crores of rupees were allegedly collected from 177 private schools on false assurances. Bank accounts linked to the accused, their family members and associates have been identified and frozen – 20 accounts linked to Arasakumar and his family and 29 accounts linked to another suspect, Muthukumar, are under financial scrutiny. CCB teams began simultaneous searches from September 15 at four locations in Chennai and Tiruchy belonging to the former minister and at two locations belonging to his aide, Valadi Karthik. Also Read: Tamil Nadu: Anti-Corruption wing books senior DMK leader KN Nehru, associates over Rs 1,020 crore tender irregularities Anbil Mahesh Poyyamozhi said after the raids, “the moment we raise questions in the Assembly or speak in public, raids follow. I had questioned in public speeches about the need to spend over Rs 1,000 crore on a new secretariat despite existing infrastructure. Soon after, this search happens. I have nothing to hide. Several documents related to his tenure as School Education Minister in the DMK regime were taken, including district-wise review files on Class 10 and 12 results and policy-related records of the education department. ‘These are official and academic records. Nothing illegal was found’.” Tiruchirappalli, Tamil Nadu: Former Minister Anbil Mahesh says, "The search was politically motivated and carried out to divert attention from my recent political statements. Searches were being conducted against those who questioned the government in the Assembly...I would... https://t.co/T763sOgrok pic.twitter.com/8j3JI5bK1t — ANI (@ANI) September 16, 2026 DMK workers protested near the residence of the former minister in Trichy, alleging that police were not allowing his team of lawyers to meet him. They also alleged that calls to the former minister were not being permitted, with even calls from advocates being blocked. It has been more than five hours, they claim, and cadres have not been allowed to meet him outside. Also Read: Unmasking Stalin empire of corruption that tarnishes Tamil honour DMK president termed the police raids and summoning as part of diversionary tactics and vendetta politics when people were agitating over unscheduled power cuts all over the state. There is no response for people missing in Nepal floods and scarcity of Aavin milk, twin murder in Ramanathapuram, murder of MTC driver in Chennai, etc. அன்பில் மகேஸ் பொய்யாமொழி மீது ரெய்டு: மற்றுமொரு திசைதிருப்பும், அரசியல் பழிவாங்கல் நடவடிக்கை ▶️ தமிழ்நாடு முழுவதும் மின்வெட்டினால் பாதிக்கப்படும் மக்களின் போராட்டங்கள் ▶️ பட்டினப்பாக்கம் மீனவர்கள் போராட்டம் ▶️ நேபாளத்தில் காணாமல் போனவர்களின் உறவினர்கள் உரிய பதில் கிடைக்காமல்... — M.K.Stalin (@mkstalin) September 16, 2026 Critics allege it has become a pattern whenever ED, IT or police conducts raids, workers are mobilised after giving money to show their muscle power. Earlier, when IT conducted a raid at Senthil Balaji’s premises, officials were assaulted, including women officers. It is still continuing and has spread to Kerala too. A dangerous trend, and now these enforcement agencies bring Central forces for security.

articles.title: Worth an Audit
articles.description: Aross the length and breadth of the country, and particularly in J&K, there is an undeniable surge in civil construction. Earth movers dot the landscape, roads are being widened, drains are being dug, and public buildings are rising from the ground. To the untrained eye, this flurry of activity paints a picture of a region on the march, a testament to developmental focus and economic momentum. However, a closer, more discerning inspection reveals a deeply unsettling reality. The civil works, ubiquitous as they are, suffer from a chronic, systemic affliction: they are overwhelmingly of a shockingly low grade. We are building at an unprecedented pace, but we are building poorly. It is a facade of progress, masking an impending infrastructural disaster that will cost the exchequer and the taxpayer dearly in the years to come. To understand why newly laid roads wash away with the first monsoon showers, or why freshly plastered walls develop cracks before a project is even officially inaugurated, one must look at the genesis of the problem: the tendering process. The root cause of this infrastructural malaise lies in the prevailing culture of contractors quoting at the absolute minimum rate. Driven by a flawed procurement ecosystem that blindly worships the L1 (lowest bidder) metric, contractors engage in a race to the bottom. In their desperation to secure tenders and outbid competitors, they quote prices that are fundamentally detached from the economic realities of sound construction. Let us be brutally clear about the arithmetic of construction: quality comes at a price. When a contractor wins a bid at a rate that barely covers the base cost of standard operations, the profit margin—and indeed, the survival margin—must be extracted from elsewhere. It is an open secret in the construction industry that an impossibly low bid is not a sign of incredible efficiency; it is a preamble to compromised quality. The government, by accepting these rock-bottom quotes without rigorously questioning their feasibility, becomes a willing accomplice in the degradation of its own infrastructure. We celebrate the financial savings on paper, completely ignoring the massive recurring costs of maintenance, repair, and premature replacement that will inevitably follow. When contractors are squeezed by the very minimum rates they themselves quoted, the immediate casualty is the material used. It is entirely obvious and utterly predictable. To make the math work, high-grade cement is routinely replaced with inferior alternatives, or the cement-to-sand ratio is cynically manipulated on site. The steel rebars, meant to provide the tensile backbone to our structures, are often of substandard gauge and quality. Bitumen on our roads is spread perilously thin, mixed with improper aggregates, and laid at incorrect temperatures to save on fuel and time. These are not victimless compromises. The use of low-quality materials directly translates to compromised structural integrity and public peril. A retaining wall built with adulterated concrete is a tragedy waiting to happen during the next heavy downpour. A road laid with insufficient bitumen becomes a series of hazardous potholes within months, endangering lives and slowing down economic activity. The contractor walks away with his profit margin intact, having fulfilled the bare minimum requirements on paper, while the public is left to navigate the crumbling remnants of so-called “development.” Yet, the minimum rate quotes and the resulting substandard materials are only symptoms of a much larger, more insidious disease. The most critical failure, the enabler of this entire charade is the glaring lack of supervision by the concerned departments. Contractors will naturally attempt to maximize their margins; it is the nature of business. But it is the sworn duty of the government departments, specifically the engineers, junior engineers, and site supervisors, to ensure that the work adheres strictly to the mandated specifications. Tragically, this supervisory mechanism has all but collapsed. Whether due to a crippling shortage of staff, institutional apathy, or a deeply entrenched nexus between the executors and the monitors, the oversight is practically non-existent. Bills are passed, and completion certificates are issued for work that barely passes a visual test, let alone rigorous quality control checks. The site supervisor is the first line of defense against substandard construction. When that defense is absent or compromised, the contractor is given a free pass to plunder the public purse through poor workmanship. The lack of on-site vigilance means that the engineering specifications detailed in the tender documents remain entirely fictional, existing only in files rather than on the ground. This brings us to the pressing situation in Jammu and Kashmir. The region is currently undergoing a massive infrastructural overhaul. From smart city projects in Srinagar and Jammu to rural road connectivity under various national schemes, hundreds of crores are being pumped into the UT. However, the whispers of discontent regarding the quality of these works are growing into a crescendo. Citizens are witnessing firsthand the slapdash manner in which drains are being constructed, roads are being patched, and public buildings are being erected. The harsh weather conditions of J&K, extreme winters, heavy snowfall, and torrential rains demand infrastructure of the highest resilience. Instead, we are getting fragile, low-grade constructions that will not survive a single harsh season. To improve the standard and quality of public work underway and infrastructure projects to follow latest standards in respective fields, we need a complete overhaul of our technical protocols. And similarly adopt Quality Standards for Audit criteria, ensuring that every assessment is measured against established national and international benchmarks rather than subjective observations. Another important aspect is training of Engineers in Government departments especially in J&K. There is hardly any training from the day a young engineer joins till his retirement. All he learns is by field experience. Upgradation of knowledge, adoption of new technologies is relevant in every engineering department else we will keep following old practices. In infrastructure development lot has changed in last 20 years. Trained engineers and upgradation in knowledge helps in better supervision of projects. State Government can use training establishments with various ministries and departments across the country. The economic ramifications of this infrastructural negligence in Jammu and Kashmir are profound. Our region relies heavily on two primary engines: tourism and agriculture. Both demand robust, reliable connectivity. When a vital arterial road connecting a tourist hotspot degrades rapidly due to low-grade bitumen and poor sub-base preparation, it is not just an inconvenience; it actively deters visitors, harming the local hospitality economy. Similarly, for the apple growers of Shopian or the saffron farmers of Pampore, every pothole on the route to the mandi translates to damaged produce and lost income. We are building infrastructure to supposedly boost these sectors, yet by allowing contractors to cut corners and by failing to supervise their work, we are actively sabotaging the very economic lifelines we aim to strengthen. The narrative of a new era cannot be built on foundations that crumble to dust at the slightest pressure. Some of the civil work currently happening in Jammu and Kashmir is, without a doubt, worth an audit. In fact, it desperately demands one. We cannot afford to squander this historic opportunity for infrastructural development on ephemeral, low-quality construction. A comprehensive, independent technical audit of all major civil works executed in the last few years is an absolute necessity. This audit must not merely look at the financial ledgers but must involve core sampling of concrete, thickness testing of roads, and a rigorous review of the materials used against the tender specifications. Accountability must be fixed not just on the contractors who executed the poor work, but equally on the officials who signed off on it. But audits take time, and the damage is being done today. Therefore, there is an immediate, actionable step that must be taken. It is high time that the senior officials of the Roads & Buildings (R&B) Department, and indeed the concerned Minister or the highest administrative authorities in the UT, step out of their secretariats. We need less boardroom planning and more on-ground inspection. A few unannounced, surprise visits to active construction sites by the top brass will send a shockwave through the system. When the highest levels of leadership demonstrate that they are invested in the quality of the work, and not just the completion of it, the entire bureaucratic machinery falls in line. The people of Jammu and Kashmir deserve infrastructure that stands the test of time, not infrastructure that requires rebuilding every two years. We must dismantle the unholy trinity of lowest-bidder obsession, substandard materials, and absent supervision. Development is not measured by the number of projects inaugurated, but by the durability and utility of the assets created. It is time to demand quality, enforce accountability, and ensure that every rupee of public money translates into solid, lasting public assets. The current state of civil works is not just a failure of engineering; it is a breach of public trust. An audit is not just warranted; it is an urgent moral imperative. Lt Gen R. S. Reen is a former DGQA

articles.title: Private hospitals await Rs 500 Cr dues
articles.description: Srinagar, Sep 18: A never before and mounting payment crisis under the Ayushman Bharat-PMJAY SEHAT scheme has once again threatening the continuity of the Government funded health insurance coverage in J&K. With private healthcare providers under severe financial strain, due to unpaid claims running into over Rs 500 crore, pending for several months, it is already a system falling apart. Many private hospitals, Greater Kashmir has learnt, have curtailed providing treatment under PMJAY SEHAT Scheme, depriving J&K citizens of insurance cover during their spells of illness. The illnesses, that were insured, and that the scheme aimed at preventing from becoming financially catastrophic, have again started haunting people. Earlier, J&K residents had the option of getting pacemakers, gall bladder surgeries, and many other surgeries from private hospitals. Now these options have shrunk. While J&K Government restricted many treatments to public hospitals only under PMJAY SEHAT Scheme, many others are being denied by hospitals as they struggle with finances. This scenario is keeping bothe the patients and empanelled hospitals on edge. While State Health Agency (SHA) has taken action against private hospitals denying treatment under SEHAT scheme in past, the hospitals are left with no option but to explore the option of exiting the scheme. More than Rs 500 crore are due from SHA to private empanelled hospitals, an insider told Greater Kashmir. The figure could not be independently verified from official records. However, it comes against the backdrop of repeated complaints from empanelled private hospitals for years, persistently. This year in June, private hospitals and dialysis centres had threatened to withdraw from the scheme from July 1. They cited delayed settlement of approved claims and mounting financial pressure that was making it difficult for them to run even their daily operations. The government subsequently sanctioned Rs 175 crore, which however was only part of the pending amount. The hospital administrators and their representatives again raised the issue in August. The payments, they said, have remained pending for around eight months. The cashless treatment continues to face recurring crises over payments, the private hospital representatives said. A representative told Greater Kashmir said the impasse is due to multiple factors. Major one is that there is funding constraint. “When SHA has funds, it starts paying public hospitals first, leaving private hospitals behind,” he said. In addition, the continuing preference for an insurance-based model for implementation is coming in way for smooth payment disbursements. “The Finance Department is reluctant to allow the scheme to be run without an insurance arrangement, There are differences involving the insurer that was selected through the tender process,” he said. Official records show that SHA-J&K has historically used an insurance model for implementation. It has undertaken tendering for selection of an insurance company, the official tender granted to Reliance General Insurance. He said there is a broader reluctance within sections of the administration to politically own a centrally sponsored health scheme. The financial consequences, meanwhile, are becoming increasingly visible. Private hospitals participating in SEHAT state they are unable to pay doctors, nurses, technicians, suppliers and other operational costs. Due to delayed reimbursement, their payments against loans are also getting defaulted. They said any prolonged accumulation of unpaid claims is potentially affecting the availability of cashless treatment itself. As of February 28, 2026, J&K had generated 87.91 lakh Ayushman cards. The records show 19.45 lakh claims had been submitted and 16.21 lakh paid.

articles.title: Business News | Cornea Unveils AI-Driven Pro AV Innovations and Next-Gen Displays at InfoComm India 2026
articles.description: Get latest articles and stories on Business at LatestLY. Mumbai (Maharashtra) [India], September 18: Cornea, a prominent Indian Pro AV and display solutions manufacturer, successfully showcased its latest innovations at InfoComm India 2026, held from September 16 to 18 at the Jio World Convention Centre in Mumbai. The company demonstrated its expanded ecosystem under the central theme, “One Brand for Every Display Need,” highlighting its commitment to providing a single, comprehensive source for hardware, software, and AI-enabled AV infrastructure across education, corporate, government, and institutional sectors.
